summaryTr: Genç bilim insanı Victor Frankenstein, cansız bir bedene hayat vermeyi başarır; ama yarattığı varlığa sırtını döndüğü an, ikisini de buzlarla kaplı kuzeye kadar sürükleyecek bir kâbus başlar. Mary Shelley'nin ünlü romanının B2 düzeyinde kısaltılmış, sadık bir anlatımı.
paragraphs: ## Letters from the Ice

My dear Margaret, I am writing to you from the far north of Russia, where my ship is almost ready to sail. For six years I have dreamed of this voyage. I want to reach the North Pole and find a passage through the ice where no one has ever been. My only sadness is that I have no friend on board, no one who shares my dreams or can tell me when I am wrong.

August. Margaret, something so strange has happened that I must write it down. Last week our ship was trapped by ice. When the fog lifted, we saw a sledge pulled by dogs crossing the ice towards the north, about half a mile away. In it sat a figure shaped like a man, but enormous, far larger than any man I have ever seen.

That night the ice broke up. In the morning my sailors were leaning over the side, talking to someone in the sea. On a floating piece of ice lay another sledge with one living dog and a man, half frozen. He was no wild giant but a European, and he spoke to us in English with a foreign accent.
"Before I come on board your ship," he said, "will you be kind enough to tell me where you are going?"

The man was close to death, and he wanted to know our direction. Only when I told him we were sailing north did he agree to come on board. He was terribly thin, and his arms and legs were nearly frozen. For two days he could not speak. Later, when my lieutenant asked why he had come so far across the ice, his face grew dark. "To find someone who ran away from me," he said.

Over the following days I came to love this stranger. He is gentle and wise, but deeply unhappy. One evening I told him I would give anything, even my life, for the knowledge I was seeking. A look of pain crossed his face. "Unhappy man!" he cried. "Do you share my madness? Then listen to my story, and learn from it." His name was Victor Frankenstein. Every night I have written down his words as closely as I can. This is his story.
## A Childhood by the Lake

My family comes from Geneva. My father, Alphonse Frankenstein, married late. My mother, Caroline, was the daughter of a poor friend of his; my father had found her weeping beside her father's coffin and had taken care of her.

When I was about five, we stayed beside Lake Como. My mother often visited the poor, and in one small cottage she found a farmer's wife feeding five hungry children. Four were dark-eyed and strong, but the fifth was a thin little girl with golden hair and clear blue eyes. She was not the farmer's child. Her mother had died, and her father, an Italian nobleman who had fought for his country's freedom, had disappeared. The girl's name was Elizabeth Lavenza, and my parents took her home with them.

The evening before she came to us, my mother had said playfully, "I have a pretty present for my Victor. He will have it tomorrow." When she gave me Elizabeth, I took her words seriously, as children do. Elizabeth was mine to protect and to love. We called each other "cousin", although we were not related by blood. She was more than a sister to me.

We grew up between Geneva and a house on the shore of the lake. Elizabeth loved the beauty of the world; I wanted to know its causes. My best friend was Henry Clerval, a merchant's son who loved stories of knights and adventure. Later two brothers were born, Ernest and little William. No child ever had a happier home.

But I had a dangerous hunger for secrets. At thirteen I discovered the books of the old alchemists, and I dreamed of banishing disease from the human body. At fifteen I watched a violent storm come over the mountains. A stream of fire burst from an old oak tree near our house, and when the light vanished, only a blasted stump remained. A visitor explained to us the power of electricity, and I was filled with wonder.

When I was seventeen, my parents decided to send me to the university of Ingolstadt in Germany. Before I could leave, Elizabeth caught scarlet fever. My mother nursed her, and although Elizabeth recovered, my mother caught the fever herself. On her deathbed she joined our hands. "My children," she said, "my firmest hopes of future happiness were placed on your marriage. Elizabeth, my love, you must take my place for the younger children." A few weeks later I left for Ingolstadt.
## The Secret of Life

The first professor I visited, M. Krempe, was a short, rough man who laughed at my old books. "Every minute you have wasted on those books is utterly lost," he told me. But a few days later I heard a lecture by M. Waldman, a gentle man with a beautiful voice. "The old masters promised impossible things and achieved nothing," he said. "Modern scientists promise very little, yet they have performed real miracles. They can even command the thunder of heaven."
As he spoke, one thought filled my mind. So much has been done, but I will achieve far more. I will explore unknown powers and show the world the deepest secrets of creation.

From that day, chemistry and natural philosophy became my whole life, and Waldman became my friend and guide. In two years I had made discoveries that were admired by the whole university. Then one question took hold of me: where does life come from? To understand life, I knew, I must first study death. I spent days and nights in vaults and graveyards, watching how the human body decays.

Then, after many exhausting nights, a sudden light broke over me. I discovered the cause of life itself. More than that, I became able to give life to lifeless matter. I will not tell you the secret, my friend. You can see what it has done to me. Learn from my example how dangerous knowledge can be.

I decided to build a human being. Because the smallest parts were so difficult to work with, I made him enormous, about eight feet tall. I collected bones from burial houses and took materials from the dissecting room and the slaughterhouse. I worked alone in a room at the top of the house. My cheeks grew pale and my body thin. I dreamed that a new race of beings would bless me as their creator.
Seasons came and went, and I did not notice them. I stopped writing to my family. Every night I had a slight fever, and the fall of a leaf made me jump like a criminal. But I could not stop.
## A Dreary Night in November

It was on a dreary night in November that I saw the result of my work. It was one o'clock in the morning; the rain was beating against the windows, and my candle had nearly burned out. I gathered the instruments of life around me, so that I could put a spark of life into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. By the dying light I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open. It breathed hard, and its arms and legs began to move.

I had chosen his features to be beautiful. Beautiful! His yellow skin hardly covered the muscles beneath it. His hair was black and flowing, his teeth as white as pearls, but these only made his watery eyes and straight black lips more horrible. I had worked for nearly two years for this moment. Now the dream vanished, and my heart filled with horror and disgust. I rushed out of the room.

At last I fell asleep in my clothes, and I dreamed of Elizabeth. I kissed her, but her lips turned the colour of death, and suddenly I was holding the body of my dead mother. I woke in a cold sweat. In the yellow moonlight I saw the creature standing by my bed. He had lifted the curtain and was staring at me. A grin wrinkled his cheeks, and one hand reached out, perhaps to stop me, but I escaped down the stairs. I spent the rest of the night in the courtyard, shaking at every sound.

In the morning I walked the wet streets for hours, afraid to go home. Outside an inn a coach stopped, and out stepped Henry Clerval! He had come to study at Ingolstadt. When we reached my rooms, I went in first, terrified that the monster would still be there. The rooms were empty. He had gone.

My relief turned into wild laughter, and then I collapsed. A fever held me for several months, and Henry nursed me through the whole winter. In my fever I talked endlessly about the monster, but Henry believed it was the illness speaking. When spring came, I slowly recovered, though the word chemistry made me tremble. Little by little, with Henry's help, I began to feel like the happy young man I had once been.
## Death in Geneva

Then a letter came from my father. "Victor," he wrote, "William is dead! That sweet child has been murdered." One warm evening in May, the family had gone for a walk at Plainpalais. William had run ahead to hide and could not be found. Early the next morning my father found him lying on the grass, dead, with the marks of the murderer's fingers on his neck. That evening William had been wearing a small portrait of my mother, and the portrait was gone.

It was dark when I reached Geneva, and the city gates were already shut, so I went to see the place where William had died. A great storm broke over the mountains, and lightning lit up the lake like a sheet of fire. Then, in one bright flash, I saw a figure among the trees, gigantic and more hideous than any human being. It was the creature I had made. At once I knew: he had murdered my brother. Before I could move, he climbed the steep rocks of Mont Salève with impossible speed and disappeared.
Who would believe my story? People would think I was mad. So I said nothing.

At home I learned that someone had already been arrested: Justine Moritz, a gentle girl who had lived with our family for years and loved William like a mother. The portrait of my mother had been discovered in her pocket. "But she is innocent!" I cried. Elizabeth believed in her too.

At the trial Justine explained that she had spent the night searching for William and had slept in a barn when the gates were closed. She could not explain how the portrait had reached her pocket. Elizabeth spoke bravely for her, but the evidence was against her, and Justine was condemned. Worse, she then confessed. When we visited her in prison, she told us the truth. "I confessed a lie," she wept. "My priest threatened me with hell until I almost believed I was the monster he said I was."
The next day Justine was executed. Two innocent people had died because of me, and I had kept silent. My guilt sat in my chest like a stone that I could not lift.
## The Sea of Ice

I could not sleep or eat. At last I set out alone for the valley of Chamonix, hoping that the great mountains would calm me. Early one morning I climbed Montanvert and walked down onto the glacier that people call the Sea of Ice. Its surface rose and fell like the waves of a stormy sea, and above it all stood Mont Blanc.

Suddenly I saw a figure crossing the ice towards me with superhuman speed, jumping over the deep cracks that I had stepped around so carefully. It was the creature. I trembled with rage. "Devil!" I shouted. "How dare you come near me? I wish I could destroy you and bring back the people you have murdered!"

"I expected this," he said calmly. "All people hate the miserable. Yet you, my creator, hate me, your own creature. Do your duty towards me, and I will do mine towards you and the rest of mankind. If you refuse, I will kill until death is satisfied with the blood of your remaining friends."

I threw myself at him, but he moved away easily. "Be calm," he said. "You made me stronger than yourself, but I will not fight you. Remember that I am your creature. I ought to be your Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel. Everywhere I see happiness, and I alone am shut out from it. I was kind and good; misery made me a devil. Make me happy, and I will be good again."
"Go away!" I said. "We are enemies."

"Listen to my story," he begged. "Even criminals are allowed to speak in their own defence. Then, if you can, destroy the work of your hands." He led me across the ice to a hut on the mountain and lit a fire. For the first time I wondered what a creator owes to his creature. I sat down, and he began his tale.
## What the Creature Saw

I remember very little of my first days. I left your rooms and found shelter in a forest near Ingolstadt. I ate berries and drank from streams. I was cold and hungry, and I sat down and cried. Then the gentle moon rose over the trees, and I felt a kind of wonder.

One day I found a fire that some travellers had left behind. I put my hand into it and cried out with pain. How strange, I thought, that the same thing could give such warmth and such pain! When food became scarce, I walked to a village, but people screamed when they saw me. Some ran away; others threw stones until I escaped, hurt and frightened. That night I found a low hovel built against the wall of a cottage. Through a crack in the wall I could see into the house. I lived there for many months.

Three people lived in the cottage: an old blind man who played sweetly on the guitar, a young man named Felix and his sister Agatha. They were poor, but they treated each other with such love that I wept as I watched them. At night I cut wood for their fire and left it at their door. They began to speak of a "good spirit" who helped them, and my heart filled with joy.

Slowly I learned their words: fire, milk, bread, wood. Then one day I saw my reflection in a pool. At first I jumped back, unable to believe that the monster in the water was me. When I understood, I was filled with the bitterest sadness.

In the spring a beautiful stranger arrived. She was Safie, the daughter of a Turkish merchant, and Felix loved her. Safie did not speak their language, so Felix began to teach her. Hidden behind my wall, I learned with her, and I learned faster. Soon I could speak and read. And I asked myself: what am I? No mother had ever smiled at me.

Later I found a leather bag in the woods with three books inside. One of them, Paradise Lost, moved me deeply. Like Adam, I had been made by a creator. But Adam had come from God's hands happy and protected, while I was alone. More often I felt like Satan, the fallen angel, burning with envy at the happiness of others.

Then, in the pocket of the coat I had taken from your laboratory, I found your journal of the four months before my creation. I read every disgusting detail of how I was made. "Cursed creator!" I cried. "Why did you make a monster so ugly that even you turned away from me in disgust?" Yet I still had hope. The cottagers were good. If I could win their friendship before they saw my face, perhaps they would accept me.
## The Door of the Cottage

I chose a day when the young people had gone for a walk and the old man sat alone. I knocked at the door. "Come in," said De Lacey, for that was his name. I told him I was a traveller who needed rest by the fire. His kindness gave me courage. I told him that I had good friends nearby who might think I was a monster when they saw me. "I am blind and cannot judge your face," he said, "but your words sound honest. Perhaps I can help."
At that moment I heard footsteps outside. I seized the old man's hand. "Now is the time!" I cried. "Save me and protect me! You and your family are the friends I am looking for!"
"Great God!" he cried. "Who are you?"

The door opened, and Felix, Safie and Agatha came in. Agatha fainted, and Safie ran out of the house. Felix tore me away from his father, threw me to the ground and struck me violently with a stick. I could have torn him to pieces as a lion tears an antelope, but my heart sank inside me and I did not fight back. I escaped to my hovel.
The next day the family left the cottage for ever. That night something broke inside me. I danced around the empty cottage with a burning branch and watched the flames destroy it.

I knew from your papers that you came from Geneva, so I travelled there, walking only at night through the long, bitter winter. One spring morning I saw a young girl slip from a river bank into the fast water. I jumped in and pulled her out. But a man ran up, tore her from my arms and, when I followed, shot me. That was my reward for saving a human life. Lying in pain, I swore eternal hatred against all mankind.

Weeks later, in a field outside Geneva, a beautiful little boy came running towards me. I thought: this child is too young to hate ugliness. I can teach him to be my friend. I caught him, but he covered his eyes and screamed. "Monster! Let me go, or I'll tell my papa. My papa is M. Frankenstein. He will punish you!"

Frankenstein! The son of my enemy! I took him by the throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet. I felt a wild, cruel joy. I too can create misery, I thought. Around his neck I found a portrait of a lovely woman. Then, in a barn, I found a young woman asleep in the straw. She would never smile at me, I thought, so let her suffer. I put the portrait into a fold of her dress and ran away.

"I am alone and miserable," the creature said at last. "No human being will live with me. But a woman as ugly as I am would not turn away from me. You must create a companion for me, a female of my own kind. That is my demand."
## Work on a Lonely Island

At first I refused angrily. He answered quietly. "Make me this companion, and we will go to the wild places of South America. We will live on acorns and berries, and no one will ever see us again. But if you refuse, you will curse the hour you were born." His words moved me. Did I not owe him a little happiness? At last I gave him my promise. "I will watch your progress," he said, and he ran down the mountain faster than an eagle flies.

At home I could not bring myself to begin. My father asked whether I still wished to marry Elizabeth. I said yes, with all my heart, but first I wanted to travel to England to learn what I needed for the work. Henry came with me. We visited London, Oxford and finally Scotland. There I left Henry with friends and went alone to one of the most distant of the Orkney Islands, a rocky place with only a few poor huts.

I began the work again. The first time I had been blinded by enthusiasm; now I saw clearly what I was doing, and it made me sick. One evening terrible thoughts came to me. What if the female was even more evil than he was? What if they hated each other? And if they had children, a whole race of devils might spread over the earth. Did I have the right to buy my own peace at such a price?

I looked up. In the moonlight, the creature was at the window, watching me with a ghastly grin. He had followed me all the way. Trembling with passion, I tore to pieces the thing I was making. He gave a howl of despair and disappeared.
Hours later he came through my door. "Do you dare to break your promise?" he said. "I have followed you through cold and hunger. You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!"
"Never," I answered. "I will never make another like you."

"Shall every man find a wife, and every beast have its mate, and I be alone?" he cried. "You can destroy my other hopes, but revenge remains. Remember this: I will be with you on your wedding night." Then he was gone, and I saw his boat shoot across the dark water.
## The Body on the Shore
So he would kill me on my wedding night, I thought. Not once did I imagine that he meant someone else.

Before dawn I put the remains of my work into a basket with heavy stones, rowed out to sea and threw it into the water. Then, exhausted, I fell asleep in the boat. When I woke, a strong wind was driving me far from land, and for hours I was at the mercy of the waves. In the evening I reached a small town on the coast of Ireland.

A crowd stood watching me land. "You must come to Mr. Kirwin," a man told me, "and give an account of yourself." Mr. Kirwin was the magistrate. A young man had been found dead on the beach the night before, with black marks of fingers on his neck, and fishermen had seen a boat like mine nearby.

They took me to see the body. It was Henry Clerval. My dearest friend, so full of life and joy, lay cold before me. "Have my evil plans taken your life too, my dearest Henry?" I cried. Then I fell into a violent fever.

For two months I lay in prison, close to death. Mr. Kirwin was kind to me, and he wrote to my father, who came at once. It was proved that I had been on the Orkney Islands when Henry was killed, and I was set free. On the journey home I said to my father wildly, "I am the murderer of William, of Justine and of Henry." He thought my illness had disturbed my mind.

In Geneva, Elizabeth welcomed me with tears. I thought of the creature's threat. If he came to fight me, I would fight him to the death. If I won, I would be free to be happy with her. So we fixed the wedding for ten days later, and from then on I carried pistols and a dagger at all times.
## The Wedding Night

The day of our wedding was bright, and for a few hours I was almost happy. After the ceremony we crossed the lake by boat to spend our first night at Evian. When we reached the inn, night fell and a heavy storm came down. A thousand fears rose in my heart. I kept one hand on the pistol hidden in my coat.
Elizabeth watched me in frightened silence. "What is it, my dear Victor?" she asked at last. "What are you afraid of?"
"Oh, peace, peace, my love," I replied. "After this night all will be safe. But this night is dreadful, very dreadful."

I begged her to go to bed, and I walked up and down the passages of the inn, searching every corner. I found nothing, and I was beginning to hope, when I heard a terrible scream from the room where Elizabeth had gone.

At that moment the whole truth rushed into my mind. I ran into the room. Elizabeth lay across the bed, lifeless, her face pale and half covered by her hair. The marks of the creature's hands were on her neck.

I looked up. The shutters had been thrown open, and in the pale yellow light of the moon I saw a hideous figure at the window. The creature was grinning, and with one finger he pointed at the body of my wife. I fired my pistol, but he jumped from the window and plunged into the lake.
Back in Geneva, my father, who had loved Elizabeth like a daughter, could not bear this last grief. A few days later he died in my arms.

For many months, I was told, I was kept in a cell as a madman. When I came back to my senses, I had only one thought left: revenge. A magistrate listened to my story but did not truly believe it. So I decided to hunt the creature myself.

Before I left Geneva, I went at night to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth and my father lay. I knelt on the grass and swore to follow the devil who had caused this misery until he or I died. A loud, terrible laugh answered me out of the darkness. Then a voice I knew whispered close to my ear: "I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied."
## The Edge of the World

For months I followed him: along the river Rhone to the Mediterranean, onto a ship bound for the Black Sea, across the wild lands of Tartary and Russia. Sometimes he left messages cut into trees or stones, because he was afraid that I would lose track of him, give up and die. "My reign is not over yet," one said. "Follow me to the everlasting ice of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, which cannot hurt me. Come on, my enemy."

At the edge of the frozen ocean I bought a sledge and dogs, and I began to gain on him. One day I saw him less than a mile ahead. But just then the ice broke with a sound like thunder, and the sea rose between us. I was left drifting on a piece of ice while my dogs died around me. Then your ship appeared. That is why I asked where you were going. If you had been sailing south, I would have stayed on the ice.
"Walton," he said when his story was finished, "if I die, swear to me that he will not escape. Swear that you will find him and kill him."

September. Margaret, our own situation is now desperate. Mountains of ice surround the ship and threaten to crush it. My sailors came and demanded that, if the ice opened, I should turn back south at once. Victor, although very weak, raised himself and spoke to them with sudden fire. "Did you not call this a glorious expedition? It was glorious because it was full of danger. Be men, or be more than men!" His words moved them, but in the end I agreed to return. I am coming back ignorant and disappointed.

When the ice broke and the way south opened, the sailors shouted with joy. Victor tried to rise from his bed. "You may give up your purpose," he said, "but I will not." But he was too weak, and he fell back. Later he called me to him. "I created a living, thinking creature, and I owed him happiness," he said. "But I owed more to my own kind, so I was right to refuse him a companion. Farewell, Walton. Seek happiness in a quiet life and avoid ambition, even the ambition of making discoveries in science. Yet why do I say this? I have failed, but another may succeed." Half an hour later he pressed my hand weakly, and his eyes closed for ever.

At midnight I heard a voice from the cabin where his body lay. I went in. Over the coffin bent a gigantic figure, his face hidden by long, ragged hair. When he heard me, he sprang towards the window. I had never seen anything so horrible as his face. I called to him to stay.

"That is also my victim!" he cried, looking down at Victor. "Oh, Frankenstein! What use is it now to ask you to forgive me, when I destroyed you by destroying everything you loved? He is cold. He cannot answer me."
"It is too late to be sorry," I said. "If you had listened to your conscience before, he would still be alive."

"Do you think I felt no pain?" he answered. "My heart was made for love, and when misery turned it to hatred, I suffered a torture that you cannot imagine. You hate me, but you cannot hate me as much as I hate myself. Do not fear that I will do any more harm. I will go to the most northern point of the earth. There I will build my funeral fire and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that no one can ever make another like me. I shall die, and I will no longer feel these agonies. Farewell!"
He jumped from the cabin window onto the ice raft that lay close to the ship. He was soon carried away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.

glossary.cousin: kuzen; burada kan bağı olmayan, evlatlık Elizabeth'e verilen sevgi sözcüğü
glossary.spark: kıvılcım; burada cansız bedene verilen 'hayat kıvılcımı'

quiz.q: What does the half-frozen stranger ask Walton before he agrees to come on board?
options: Whether there is a doctor on the ship
Who the captain of the ship is
Where the ship is going
Whether the sailors have seen a giant
quiz.explainTr: Victor gemiye binmeden önce geminin nereye gittiğini sorar; çünkü güneye gidiyorsa buzda kalıp yaratığı kovalamaya devam edecektir.

quiz.q: How did Elizabeth become part of the Frankenstein family?
options: Victor's parents adopted her after finding her in a poor farmer's cottage
She was the daughter of Victor's uncle
She came to work for the family as a servant
Her father, an old friend, left her in their care before he died in Geneva
quiz.explainTr: Victor'un annesi, Como Gölü yakınında yoksul bir çiftçinin evinde Elizabeth'i bulur ve aile onu evlat edinir; Victor'la kan bağı yoktur.

quiz.q: How does the creature learn to speak and read?
options: Victor teaches him in the laboratory
An old man in a village school teaches him
He studies Victor's journal from the first day
He secretly listens while Felix teaches Safie
quiz.explainTr: Yaratık, kulübenin duvarındaki çatlaktan izlerken Felix'in Safie'ye verdiği dersleri dinleyerek konuşmayı ve okumayı öğrenir.

quiz.q: Why does Victor destroy the female creature on the Orkney Islands?
options: Henry Clerval discovers his secret work
He fears that the two creatures might bring more evil and suffering into the world
The materials he needs are stolen
Elizabeth writes and asks him to stop
quiz.explainTr: Victor, dişi yaratığın daha kötü olabileceğinden ve ikisinin çocuklarının insanlığı tehdit edebileceğinden korkar; pencerede yaratığı görünce yaptığı şeyi parçalar.

quiz.q: What does the creature say he will do at the end of the story?
options: Return to Geneva and live near Victor's grave
Find the De Lacey family again
Go to the far north and burn his own body
Stay on Walton's ship and sail to England
quiz.explainTr: Yaratık, dünyanın en kuzey noktasına gidip kendi cenaze ateşini yakacağını ve bedenini kül edeceğini söyler, sonra buz salıyla karanlıkta kaybolur.
